blocks.title: From the clock to life after approval

summary.title: Who decides
points: A marketing authorisation is the licence to sell one specific medicine.
Central track: EMA's CHMP assesses, the Commission decides; one licence for the EU plus Iceland, Liechtenstein and Norway.
National track: each NCA (BfArM, ANSM, AEMPS…) grants its own licence; the CMDh coordinates MRP and DCP.
A potential serious public-health risk goes to the CMDh for 60 days, then the CHMP and a Commission decision.
Switzerland is outside: Swissmedic grants Swiss licences.

exercises.scenario: Your generic goes through a DCP in Germany, France and Italy.

questions.prompt: Who grants the licences?
options: The European Commission, one licence covering all three countries
Each national agency, one licence per country
questions.explanation: DCP is the national track.

questions.prompt: France raises a potential serious risk to public health. Where does it go first?
options: Straight to the European Court of Justice
Back to the RMS for a new Day 0
To the CMDh, which has 60 days
questions.explanation: Then to the CHMP and a binding Commission decision if unresolved.

exercises.scenario: Sales asks whether the EU licence lets you sell in Switzerland.

questions.prompt: What's the answer?
options: No: Swissmedic grants Swiss licences separately
Yes, but only for centrally authorised products
Yes: Switzerland recognises all EU licences automatically
questions.explanation: Switzerland isn't part of the EU system.

questions.prompt: Which body coordinates multi-country national procedures?
options: The largest NCA in the procedure
questions.explanation: Its best-practice guides describe how MRP and DCP run.

summary.title: Procedures compared
points: Legal basis sets what data; the procedure sets which agencies assess.
National: one country, 210 days. Two or more countries need MRP or DCP.
MRP: an existing licence is recognised; 90 + 90 days.
DCP: no licence yet; 120 + 90 days, then 30 for national licences.
Centralised: mandatory for some products, optional for others; 210 days then a Commission decision.

exercises.scenario: You want a new generic in five EU countries and have no licence anywhere.

questions.prompt: Which procedure fits?
options: Centralised, because five countries is a lot
questions.explanation: No licence yet, several countries.

questions.prompt: You already hold a German licence and want to add Austria and Poland. Which procedure?
options: National procedures in Austria and Poland
MRP, with Germany as the lead country
A Type II variation of the German licence
questions.explanation: MRP recognises an existing licence.

exercises.scenario: A manager asks why regulatory is the most predictable segment of the plan.

questions.prompt: What's the reason?
options: The DCP has a fixed legal clock
Authorities always approve generics on the first round
The PM can book the approval date in advance
questions.explanation: 120 + 90 + 30 days, plus clock-stops.

questions.prompt: Which products can use the centralised procedure as generics?
options: Only generics made in the EU
Any generic filed in more than ten countries
questions.explanation: Optional for them; mandatory for some product types.

summary.title: Choosing RMS and CMS
points: RMS leads and writes the assessment; CMS review, comment and approve or object.
MRP: the RMS is the country that granted the licence. DCP: you propose one, and it must accept.
Practice criteria: capacity and slots, timeline record, product experience, fees and language, key markets.
CMS are the countries where you want a licence; add later through repeat use.
RMS slots are often booked months ahead: an early milestone.

exercises.scenario: You're planning a DCP for submission in nine months.

questions.prompt: What should you secure early?
questions.explanation: Slots are often booked months ahead.

questions.prompt: Which is not a usual criterion for choosing the RMS?
options: Which country has the biggest wholesaler
The agency's experience with the product type
The agency's track record on timelines
questions.explanation: The criteria are about the agency and your key markets.

exercises.scenario: Six months after the DCP closed, BD wins a partner in Portugal.

questions.prompt: How do you add Portugal?
options: A national procedure in Portugal only
questions.explanation: A follow-on MRP using the same assessment.

questions.prompt: What would have avoided the second round?
options: Closing the DCP at Day 120 instead of Day 210
Planning the full CMS list upfront
questions.explanation: The CMS list is a business decision.

summary.title: The CTD dossier
points: The CTD is the ICH dossier structure; only Module 1 differs by region.
Module 1 regional forms and texts; Module 2 summaries; Module 3 quality.
Module 4 non-clinical (mostly the reference's for a generic); Module 5 clinical (mainly BE).
The EU requires eCTD; each change adds a new sequence.
Module 1 is country by country; Module 3 quality drives the number of questions.

exercises.scenario: An assessor asks where the API specifications and stability data are.

questions.prompt: Which module?
questions.explanation: Quality: substance, product, controls, stability.

questions.prompt: Where is the bioequivalence report?
questions.explanation: Clinical study reports.

exercises.scenario: After approval, the shelf life is extended by a variation.

questions.prompt: How does the eCTD record it?
options: Only in a paper annex to the licence
By replacing the whole dossier with a new version
As a new sequence added to the dossier
It doesn't; the eCTD is frozen at approval
questions.explanation: The eCTD has a lifecycle.

questions.prompt: Which module mostly comes from the dossier owner and decides how many questions you'll get?
questions.explanation: Its quality decides the question count.

summary.title: Gap analysis
points: Compares a received dossier with current EU requirements; each shortfall becomes a task.
Checks: legal basis, EU reference BE, stability under EU conditions, ASMF or CEP, validation, nitrosamines.
Also: EU GMP status of every site, Module 1 country needs, eCTD format.
Two kinds: gaps that block filing, and likely questions that add a clock-stop later.
Blocking gaps set the earliest submission date; ask the dossier owner for dates, not promises.

exercises.scenario: The gap analysis finds only six months of stability data under EU conditions.

questions.prompt: How do you treat it?
options: As a likely question to answer in the clock-stop
As a gap that likely blocks filing, on the critical path
As a minor point for the national phase
As not relevant, since the reference product is stable
questions.explanation: Missing stability data typically block filing.

questions.prompt: The site list includes one testing lab with no EU GMP evidence. Who looks at it with RA?
questions.explanation: RA owns the gap analysis, with QA for site and quality points.

exercises.scenario: The dossier owner says 'the missing data will come soon'.

questions.prompt: What does the process card advise?
options: File without them and explain in the cover letter
questions.explanation: Slow answers from the dossier owner are a classic slip.

questions.prompt: What makes a gap list useful for planning?
options: Sorting it by the CTD module each gap belongs to
Sending it to the authority before filing
questions.explanation: That tells you which gaps sit on the critical path.

summary.title: The DCP clock
points: Day 0 after validation; preliminary assessment around Day 70; CMS comments by Day 100.
Around Day 105, the consolidated questions arrive and the clock stops.
Day 120: draft assessment report and texts; can close here if all agree.
Step II: comments around 145, outstanding issues around 180, close by Day 210.
Real duration is 210 days plus clock-stops; prepared responses shorten them.

exercises.scenario: Day 105 questions ask for 12-month stability data and an updated dissolution method.

questions.prompt: What's the PM's biggest lever now?
questions.explanation: Procedure days are fixed; the pause is yours.

questions.prompt: What should have been done before Day 105?
options: Ask the RMS to skip Step II
questions.explanation: The clock-stop is the biggest variable in the DCP.

exercises.scenario: Two similar generics filed the same month got licences five months apart.

questions.prompt: What most likely explains it?
questions.explanation: Answering faster is what shortens a DCP.

questions.prompt: When can a DCP end at Day 120?
options: When the clock-stop is under 30 days
Never; every DCP runs to Day 210
questions.explanation: Then Step II is skipped.

summary.title: The national phase
points: After the DCP closes, each country still issues its own licence.
Send high-quality translations of SmPC, leaflet and labelling within the CMDh deadline.
Countries check national details; then 30 days to grant the licence.
Licence isn't launch: you still need artwork, pricing or tenders, and QP-released stock.
Book translators before Day 120; run artwork in parallel.

exercises.scenario: The DCP closed on Day 210 last week.

questions.prompt: What's next for each country?
options: Nothing; the DCP close is the licence
Translations, national checks, then a licence within 30 days
A CMDh referral, which every DCP goes through before licences
questions.explanation: The national phase.

questions.prompt: What should already be booked?
questions.explanation: Book them before Day 120.

exercises.scenario: The CEO says 'licence next month, so we launch next month'.

questions.prompt: What else stands between licence and first sale?
options: Artwork and printed packs, pricing or tender, QP-released stock
Nothing, once the licence is granted
Only the PSMF update, since everything else came with the licence
questions.explanation: Licence is a milestone, not the finish line.

questions.prompt: How do you keep the licence-to-launch gap short?
options: Run artwork in parallel with the national phase
Start artwork after the licence is granted
questions.explanation: Parallel work keeps the gap small.

summary.title: Variations
points: Any change to a licence needs a variation, classed by risk.
IA: do and tell; most now in an annual update (since 15 Jan 2026).
IB: tell, wait 30 days, do. II: approval first, usually about 60 days. Extensions: like a new application.
Grouping bundles changes; worksharing covers one change across several licences.
Supply changes often need IB or II approval before shipping: put them on the critical path.

exercises.scenario: The manufacturer wants to add a new API supplier before the second commercial batch.

questions.prompt: What do you ask RA first?
options: Which variation type, and how long until the material can be used
Whether the CMS list must be updated
Whether the QPPV needs to change
Whether the five-year renewal date moves because of the change
questions.explanation: Classify against the current guidelines.

questions.prompt: If it's a Type II, when may you use the new supplier?
options: Straight away, then report it in the next annual update
After approval, usually about 60 days of assessment
questions.explanation: Approval comes before implementing.

exercises.scenario: The same shelf-life change is needed on licences in 12 countries.

questions.prompt: Which tool avoids 12 separate assessments?
questions.explanation: One assessment, several licences.

questions.prompt: Why should RA re-check older classifications?
options: The framework changed in 2025–2026, moving several changes lower
The CMDh reclassifies every change each year
questions.explanation: Regulation amended 2025; new guidelines 2026.

summary.title: Renewals and the sunset clause
points: Today a licence is valid 5 years and is renewed once; file at least 9 months before expiry.
After one renewal it's usually indefinite, unless PV reasons require one more.
Sunset clause: lapses if not marketed within 3 years of approval, or off the market 3 years in a row.
Generics often file in more countries than they launch: watch those licences.
Track per country: licence date, first placed on market, renewal deadline, time off market.

exercises.scenario: Your DCP granted six licences in 2025; you launched in four.

questions.prompt: What's the risk for the other two?
options: They lapse after 5 years without renewal only
They lapse if not marketed within 3 years of approval
None, as long as the RMS licence stays active and is renewed
They move automatically to your partner
questions.explanation: The sunset clock starts at approval.

questions.prompt: When must the renewal be filed for a licence granted in March 2025?
options: Only if a PV issue arises
questions.explanation: At least 9 months before the 5-year expiry.

exercises.scenario: A product was withdrawn from Belgium in 2024 for commercial reasons.

questions.prompt: When does the Belgian licence lapse if nothing changes?
options: After 3 consecutive years off the market
At the next five-year renewal, if it isn't filed in time
questions.explanation: The sunset clause also covers time off the market.

questions.prompt: What tracking tool does the lesson suggest?
options: A per-country table kept up to date
questions.explanation: Simple is fine, if it's current.

summary.title: Pharmacovigilance at launch
points: The MAH collects, assesses and acts on suspected side effects from the first pack.
PSMF describes the PV system; a QPPV lives and works in the EU.
Cases go to EudraVigilance: serious within 15 days, non-serious within 90.
Generics: RMP aligned with the reference; PSURs usually exempt unless required.
Launch checklist: QPPV named, PSMF updated, PV agreements signed, EMA product data entered.

exercises.scenario: A pharmacist reports a serious suspected side effect to your company.

questions.prompt: By when must it reach EudraVigilance?
questions.explanation: Serious cases: 15 days.

questions.prompt: Your partner received it first. Which document sets how fast they forward it?
questions.explanation: Module 0, Lesson 3.

exercises.scenario: Two weeks before launch, the PV checklist is half done.

questions.prompt: Which item is not on it?
options: A new PSUR for the generic
PSMF updated to include the product
questions.explanation: Generics are usually exempt from PSURs.

questions.prompt: How is a generic's RMP usually built?
options: It isn't needed, since generics are exempt from risk management plans
Copied from the API supplier's file
Aligned with the reference product's safety concerns
From a new clinical safety study
questions.explanation: Required, but lighter.

summary.title: Agencies, procedures and the dossier
points: Most generics take the national track: NCAs grant licences, the CMDh coordinates.
DCP for no licence yet (120 + 90 + 30 days); MRP to recognise an existing one.
The RMS leads and writes the report; book its slot early. CMS are your target countries.
CTD: Module 1 regional, 3 quality, 5 clinical (BE for a generic); eCTD sequences.
Gap analysis sorts shortfalls into 'blocks filing' and 'likely question'.

exercises.scenario: You've in-licensed a dossier written for India and want licences in six EU countries.

questions.prompt: Which sequence of first steps fits?
options: Gap analysis, book an RMS slot, prepare a DCP
Wait for the dossier owner to update the dossier
File an MRP with the Indian licence as reference
questions.explanation: No EU licence yet, so DCP; the gap analysis sets the filing date.

questions.prompt: The gap analysis lists missing EU-reference BE. What kind of gap?
options: Not a gap for a generic
questions.explanation: BE against an EU reference is required to file.

questions.prompt: Explain to a BD colleague the difference between the legal basis and the procedure.
questions.modelAnswer: The legal basis (Module 1) decides what data the dossier needs. The procedure decides which agencies assess it and in what order: national, MRP, DCP or centralised.

exercises.scenario: An assessor's question concerns the dissolution specification.

questions.prompt: Which CTD module will you update?
questions.explanation: Quality: controls and specifications.

questions.prompt: Which agency writes the assessment report?
questions.explanation: The CMS review and comment.

summary.title: From the clock to life after approval
points: DCP: questions around Day 105, draft report at 120, close by 210; clock-stops are yours.
National phase: translations, checks, licence within 30 days; licence isn't launch.
Variations (IA, IB, II, extension) must be approved before supply changes ship.
Renewal once after 5 years; the sunset clause kills unused licences after 3 years.
PV ready on day one: QPPV, PSMF, SDEAs, EudraVigilance timelines, EMA product data.

exercises.scenario: A DCP is at Day 105. The site also plans a new API supplier for launch stock.

questions.prompt: Which two items go on the critical path?
options: The renewal and the sunset date
The PSUR and the RMP update
The clock-stop responses and the variation for the new supplier
questions.explanation: Both decide when compliant stock can ship.

questions.prompt: When can the new supplier's material be used if it's Type IB?
options: Immediately, as long as the variation has been submitted
Only after a full new DCP
questions.explanation: Tell, wait and do.

questions.prompt: List the three things you still need between national licence and first sale.
questions.modelAnswer: Approved artwork with packs printed correctly; pricing and reimbursement or a tender win where relevant; and stock released by the QP and shipped.

exercises.scenario: Three years after approval, an audit finds two countries never launched and no PV agreement with one distributor.

questions.prompt: What's the licence risk?
options: The two unused licences may have lapsed under the sunset clause
Nothing, as long as the PSMF is current
questions.explanation: 3 years from approval without marketing.

questions.prompt: Why does the missing PV agreement matter?
options: Safety reports may not reach you in time for the 15/90-day deadlines
It blocks the five-year renewal of every licence in the procedure
questions.explanation: The SDEA sets how and how fast safety data move.

summary.title: Regulatory pathway: the whole picture
points: NCAs grant licences on the national track; the CMDh coordinates; Switzerland is separate.
DCP for a new multi-country generic: RMS leads, 120 + 90 + 30 days plus clock-stops.
CTD structure with eCTD sequences; gap analysis first, sorted by blocking or likely question.
Clock-stops are the variable you control; national phase and artwork run in parallel.
After approval: variations before supply changes, renewal, sunset clause.
PV system in place before the first pack.

exercises.scenario: You lead a generic from in-licensing to launch in Germany, France, Spain and Italy.

questions.prompt: Which procedure and lead country decision come first?
options: MRP, with France as the RMS that granted the licence
DCP, with an RMS slot booked early
questions.explanation: No licence yet; slots are booked months ahead.

questions.prompt: Your plan shows 210 days for the DCP. What's missing?
options: Nothing; 210 days is the real duration
questions.explanation: Real duration is 210 days plus clock-stops.

questions.prompt: After the licence, what still has to be ready for the first pack to be sold?
options: Artwork, pricing or tender, released stock, and PV
Only the national licence number on the carton
questions.explanation: Licence is a milestone, not the finish line.

exercises.scenario: Eighteen months after launch, the company changes its API supplier and drops Spain.

questions.prompt: What does the supplier change need?
options: Only an update to the PSMF
A classified variation approved before using the material
Nothing, if the API is the same substance
A new DCP, since the API supplier is part of the original assessment
questions.explanation: Often IB or II.

questions.prompt: What happens to the Spanish licence if it stays off the market?
options: It's transferred to the RMS until the product returns to the market
It lapses after 3 consecutive years off the market
It is kept forever after the first launch
questions.explanation: Sunset clause.

questions.prompt: In two sentences, explain why the DCP is the most predictable part of the plan, and what still makes it vary.
questions.modelAnswer: Its procedure days are fixed by law and the CMDh guide: 120 + 90 days and 30 national days. What varies is the clock-stops, which depend on how fast and how well the applicant answers the questions.
